name: ln
description: Creates links between files: hard links that point to the same inode, or symbolic links that point to a path.

flags.description: Create a symbolic (soft) link instead of a hard link.
Remove existing destination files before creating the link.
Print the name of each link created.
Ask before removing existing destination files.

examples.explanation: Creates a symbolic link so the app command resolves to the current release — a common deployment pattern.

examples.output:
131073 -rw-r--r-- 2 user user 220 Jan 10 09:15 file-hard.txt
131073 -rw-r--r-- 2 user user 220 Jan 10 09:15 file.txt
examples.explanation: Creates a hard link (shown via ls -li). Both names share the same inode (131073) and the link count is 2. Editing either file affects the same data.
The standard nginx pattern: enable a site by symlinking its config, replacing any existing link.
Creates a relative symlink. Relative links keep working if the whole tree is moved; absolute links do not.

about: A hard link is another directory entry referencing the same inode — the same physical data. It cannot cross filesystems or point to directories. A symbolic link is a small file containing a path; it can cross filesystems, point to directories, and dangle if the target is removed.
Deleting the original file leaves hard links fully functional (the data lives until the last link is removed), but breaks symbolic links.
useCases: Expose versioned application directories under stable paths.
Enable/disable service configs by managing symlinks (nginx, systemd wants).
Save disk space by hard-linking identical files.
mistakes: Creating a symlink with a wrong target path and not noticing — ls -l shows broken links in red.
Forgetting -s and accidentally hard-linking when a symlink was intended.
warnings: Recursive tools (cp -r, rsync, find) treat symlinks differently; learn their follow/deref options before copying trees containing links.
